caption:
True…but there’s a plot twist. 

According to Yale School of Medicine, during pregnancy, biological age increased by about 2 years. It makes sense. The sheer metabolic and physiological demands of growing a human naturally accelerates aging at the cellular level.⁠
⁠
But here’s the surprise. At three months postpartum, women’s biological age didn’t just stop increasing, it completely declined. For some, their biological age dropped by as much as 8 years compared to late pregnancy, which can be attributed to: ⁠
⁠
✨ Body Mass Index (BMI): Starting your pregnancy at a higher weight can make it harder for your cells to recover.⁠
⁠
✨ Breastfeeding: Exclusively breastfeeding can biologically fast-forward your recovery.⁠
⁠
The unknown: Lead researcher Kieran O’Donnell noted that they aren’t sure if the body is just returning to its pre-pregnancy baseline or if pregnancy leaves you biologically younger than when you started. ⁠
⁠
Only time will tell. ⁠

caption:
In some parts of the world, aging means doing the impossible.⁠
⁠
Imagine being 80 years-old free diving 65 feet underwater (with no oxygen tank) to harvest abalone, conch, seaweed, sea urchin and octopus. ⁠
⁠
Holding their breath for up to two minutes, these are the Haenyeo women of Jeju Island. They’re part of a 400-year-old tradition born from survival and necessity, where many began diving as young as 11.⁠
⁠
But this living legacy is slowly disappearing as younger generations are choosing universities and safer careers. ⁠
⁠
Today, we learn from these keepers of tradition and the incredible strength and endurance it takes to do this every day. 💙⁠
⁠

caption:
Crumbl just launched “Dirty Sodas.” Finally, some honest marketing.

One of these drinks contains 186 grams of sugar. For reference, that’s equivalent to:

- Almost 5 cans of Coke
- 2 pints of Ben & Jerry’s
- 29 Krispy Kreme donuts
- 40 Oreos

...except you’re drinking it through a straw.

The American Heart Association recommends no more than 25 grams of added sugar per day for women and 36 grams for men.

This one drink delivers roughly 5 to 7 days’ worth of added sugar in a single sitting.

And your body knows it.

When you consume that much sugar at once, your blood sugar spikes violently, triggering a massive insulin response. Your liver gets flooded with fructose it can’t process, converting it directly to fat. Your dopamine system lights up like a slot machine, making you crave more. 

This is a metabolic wrecking ball that sets the stage for insulin resistance, fatty liver disease, type 2 diabetes, and chronic inflammation.

“Dirty Soda” might be the most accurate product name I’ve seen all year.

Please do not drink this.

On the flip side, chronic stress, isolation, or conflict triggers the expression of pro-inflammatory genes, accelerating aging and increasing your risk of chronic illness.

Love and connection are powerful for health and longevity.

caption:
It’s not science fiction. As mitochondria convert nutrients into energy (ATP), they release tiny bursts of light called ultraweak photon emissions (UPE), too faint to see with the naked eye.⁠
⁠
But scientists are discovering this light may be more than just a byproduct of cellular activity.⁠
⁠
In a 2023 study, researchers stressed one group of isolated mitochondria while keeping another group unstressed. Even though the two groups couldn’t touch or exchange chemicals, the unstressed mitochondria still changed their behavior — suggesting mitochondria may communicate through light-based signals.⁠
⁠
TLDR: Mitochondria aren’t just powerhouses of the cell, they’re shaping up to be dynamic communicators, constantly sensing and responding to their environment. ⁠
⁠
Source: Mould, Rhys R., et al. “Non-chemical Signalling Between Mitochondria.” Frontiers in Physiology, September 22, 2023, Volume 14, Article 1268075. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2023.1268075/full ⁠

We've officially lost the plot. 

Mountain Dew donuts. Beer-flavored chips. Dirty soda coffee creamer. Cinnabon bacon jerky, chcolate energy drinks...?

Big Food is competing to make their products more addictive, more convenient, more profitable, and more impossible to ignore.

Turn these packages over and you'll often find the same cast of characters:

• Artificial food dyes linked to behavioral concerns in children.
• Emulsifiers like polysorbate 80, carboxymethylcellulose, mono- and diglycerides that disrupt the gut microbiome and intestinal barrier...
• "Natural flavors"—a catch-all term that can represent dozens of undisclosed flavoring compounds.
• Refined starches, high-fructose corn syrup, maltodextrin, preservatives, gums, and additives engineered to maximize shelf life and keep you reaching for another bite.

None of these ingredients are there because they make food more nutritious.

They're there because they make food more marketable.

Food should fuel your cells, support your microbiome, stabilize your blood sugar, and provide your body with the nutrients it needs to thrive.

caption:
VIEWING MORNING SUNLIGHT GETS YOU THE BIGGEST HEALTH PAYOFF FOR THE AMOUNT OF TIME INVESTED: 5-10 MINUTES POSITIVELY CHANGES YOUR BIOLOGY & PSYCHOLOGY FOR 24 HOURS (!) •
-
No other activities create the kind of positive shifts in health that viewing morning sunlight does *for the time invested*. Viewing bright light, ideally from sunlight for just a few minutes each morning, shifts your hormones and neurotransmitters in ways that significantly improve your daytime mood, focus, and alertness, and immune system function, and improve your nighttime sleep. That’s a huge payoff for just a couple of minutes of time! Also, it costs nothing and is pleasant.
-
You do need to get outside to do it, meaning through a window won’t work, and you want to take your sunglasses off. Eye eyeglasses & contacts are fine. Blink as needed to protect your eyes.
-
Keep in mind that you especially want to get morning sunlight viewing on overcast days because those days tend to be correlated with colder weather and being inside more and even though artificial lights might seem bright they’re not going to give you the kind of photon levels that you need. 
-
NOTE: when you don’t get enough bright light during the day, it sets you up for disrupted sleep from even a small amount of bright light at night, such as from screens. 
-
And of course, exercise is critical and powerful, nutrition is critical, hydration is critical,. All of those things still matter. But you’re far more likely to do those things correctly if you’ve got your circadian biology correct. And the best way to do that is to get that morning sunlight, ideally in the first hour or two after waking.
-
You don’t need to see the sunrise but # if you do, it’s great. 
-
Most people’s circadian biology is out of whack, but it’s easy and zero cost to fix. So get that morning sunlight!
-
And as always, thank you for your interest in science!

caption:
Taking care of yourself is never something to apologize for.

I say this because one of the most powerful things I have learned in 30 years of medicine is that community and connection are among the most important pillars of health there are. The people in your life, the meals you share, the late nights laughing — that is medicine too.

But so is sleep. So is movement. So is the food you put in your body every single day.

You do not have to choose between having fun and taking care of yourself. You can do both. You can be the person who orders the grilled salmon and still closes down the restaurant with your friends. You can skip the drinks and still be the life of the party. You can leave a little early and still be a great friend.

The people who love you will not remember whether you had a drink at the barbecue. They will remember that you showed up, that you were present, that you were you.

Take care of your body this summer. Spend time with the people you love. Do both without guilt.

Your health does not need anyone's approval.

caption:
GRIP STRENGTH & LONGEVITY: “LIVE HANGS” 

Congratulations Ann Crile Esselstyn, who at *90 years and 231 days* old (title card says 93), did a continual bar grip hang for 2 minutes and 52 seconds. (And set a @guinnessworldrecords WR)

Grip strength and grip endurance (not exactly the same thing) are correlates of longevity. They are great to train for but grip strength alone does not extend life. So what do they reflect?

We often think about the muscle aspect of grip. To me,the really interesting data = the relationship between grip and longevity of *cognitive functioning*.

Why would there be a relationship there?

In neuroscience, we refer to the upper and the lower motor neurons. Upper motor neurons are in the brain and are involved in deliberate action (among other things); lower motor neurons are in the spinal cord and directly connect to the muscles by extending out of the central nervous system into the peripheral nervous system. They directly cause muscles to contract.

We also think about proximal muscles, which are the muscle muscles near the midline and distal muscles like those tips of your calves, forearms, fingers and toes.

Early but compelling evidence suggest that distal strength— the motor neuron control of the parts of your body furthest from your midline, is one of the first things to atrophy as you age. 

You can offset this with strong, gripping, keeping your feet, strong, calves, etc.

So while it’s important to train your core and the muscles of your legs, chest back and arms, don’t forget about feet yes feet! 

And hands and forearms. It’s not just about aesthetics. It’s very likely about maintaining those upper motor brain neurons. 

Once specific sets of neurons in the brain start to die off they often take others with them, the so-called bystander effect.

More on this in a Huberman Lab podcast to come but meanwhile, wherever you’re at in your fitness in longevity training the whole body and keep going! And congrats to Ann. That’s a super impressive timing at any age!

caption:
Syrniki reinvented😜
One of my favourite Slavic desserts is Syrniki. It is made with curd cheese. They usually give them a round, slightly flattened shape and fry them in the pan one by one, but I decided to give Syrniki a European touch and baked them in cupcake cases in the oven. Less hassle, more enjoyment😉 

The recipe is very easy. The only thing is the curd cheese itself which you can buy only in Slavic shops in London. Brits don't usually have it.
I bought 2 packs (250gr each) of Polish curd cheese, they call it twarog, which is the same in other Slavic languages. 1 egg, 3-4 tb. spoons of erythritol (I don't use sugar any more to keep my blood sugar levels normal), 3 tb. spoons of oat flour, and a dash of vanilla syrup. Mix it with a blender, and that's it!
Then you just put the mixture into the cupcake cases and bake in the oven(180° for 25 mins). Take them out and let to cool down. Turn them over and serve with any topping. My fav is soured cream. This recipe makes 12 syrniks. Enjoy! 😁😋😊✨️✨️
Переосмысление сырников😜
Один из моих любимых славянских десертов — сырники. Он готовится из творога. Обычно им придают круглую, слегка приплюснутую форму и обжаривают на сковороде по одному, но я решила придать сырникам европейский колорит и запекла их в формочках для кексов в духовке. Меньше хлопот, больше удовольствия😉 

Рецепт очень простой. Единственное, что нужно — это сам творог, который можно купить только в славянских магазинах в Лондоне. У британцев его обычно нет.
Я купила 2 пачки (по 250 г) польского творога, его называют twarog, что то же самое и в других славянских языках. 1 яйцо, 3-4 ст. ложки эритритола (я больше не использую сахар, чтобы поддерживать нормальный уровень сахара в крови), 3 ст. ложки овсяной муки и немного ванильного сиропа. Смешиваю блендером, и все!
 Затем просто положите смесь в формочки для кексов и выпекайте в духовке (180° в течение 25 минут). Достаньте их и дайте остыть. Переверните и подавайте с любой начинкой. Мой любимый вариант — сметана. По этому рецепту получается 12 сырников. Наслаждайтесь! 😁😋😊✨️✨️

STIMULATE MUSCLE GROWTH PROPERLY: 
BACK DAY WITH @thedorianyates (6 time Mr. Olympia) •

Comment BACK & I’ll DM you a link to a video of the full workout @goldsgym.venice 

There are a lot of studies and examples of different ways to train with weights for muscle growth and strength. Which is best? 

Everyone has different opinions on that but what works best for me has been low volume high intensity training. (And when I say “best”, I mean getting the results of directed muscle growth and strength improvements and not having my nervous system feel so fried that I can’t do other things after training… after all, we have lives to live!)

It involves training 3 days per week & each muscle directly 1X per week. Yes only once. You do 1 light set & 1 moderate set just to get the mechanics and blood flow going, then 1 (maybe 2) all out sets to failure *in excellent form* which means controlling the weight all the way up, contracting it hard and lowering it slowly. Depending on the muscle group, you do anywhere from 2 to 4 exercises per muscle group total. 

6 time Mr. Olympia @thedorianyates is my guest on the Huberman Lab podcast out now and we discussed this style of training and the types of training that work best for the everyday person. That means men & women of all ages. He gives a wealth of info.

Dorian was also kind enough to take me through his version of low volume high intensity training. I got to feel what it is to target the back and rear delt muscles properly with true high intensity.

We did:

1) lat pullovers: one light set, one medium set, and then one all outset to failure (w/ a few assisted repetitions).

2) reverse grip cable pull downs (also one set to failure)

3) one arm dumbbell rows (one set to failure for each side)

4) seated wide grip cable rows (one set to failure with a couple of assisted reps)

5) rear delt bent over dumbbell raises (one warm-up and one works set to failure).

caption:
As most of you are likely aware, last weekend it was announced that former President Joe Biden had been diagnosed with stage 4 (i.e., metastatic) prostate cancer. Putting politics and conspiracy theories aside, and speaking strictly from a medical perspective, the news is nothing short of a tragic demonstration of Medicine 2.0 at its worst.

Prostate cancer is one of the very few forms of cancer for which metastasis, and therefore mortality, are almost entirely preventable. Thus, news of such advanced disease in anyone is unacceptable in my mind. But the fact that this occurred in a man who presumably was receiving the best possible medical care — a man whose health had, until recently, been a matter of national security — underscores a bitter truth: despite our ability to catch and treat prostate cancer well before it spreads, this form of cancer remains the second leading causing of cancer deaths among men. Around 35,000 men die of prostate cancer each year in the United States alone, and most of those deaths are preventable. Tragic indeed.

As such, I’d like to take this high-profile case as an opportunity to try to make some small dent in those numbers. caption:
MUCH OF LEARNING (IN DOGS & HUMANS) IS TOP DOWN INHIBITION •

Much of learning involves adjusting the connections between the prefrontal cortex and deeper brain structures that control impulses. Indeed, if you look at motor learning in humans or other mammals, you’ll notice that most of building a skill is about eliminating incorrect aspects of a movement.

This is my second bulldog mutt, and as with the last one (Costello) I started the training early at 9 weeks. 

Strummer is doing a great job learning to suppress his impulse to move aka “sit” and to come when called, to stay calm around food and all the rest. 

Dogs have a tiny prefrontal cortex relative to humans but they can multipurpose it to learn lots of things and lots of different scenarios. They are oh so smart. But it is kind of fun to think about how they’re training you as well.

Indeed training a bulldog breed (because they’re so stubborn) is also about training yourself in patience. Strummer is part mastiff and boxer/pit too but he’s still been giving us a run for our money on the patience side! What he doesn’t know is I’ve done this before. And it’s been pure pleasure.

NOTE: I want to be thoughtful in sharing any post about a bulldog and how great they are because they have wonderful personalities, but they are not trivial to raise properly and take care of properly so if you decide to take that on understand it will take many hours per day or more to train them up and to keep them healthy. If they’re just allowed to sleep and you let them just kind of move around like sea turtles they get very unhealthy and unhappy. 

I suggest getting a mutt because they tend to be a little bit easier, but then they’ll also have more energy. So then you’ve got a stubborn high energy dog! But they have huge hearts, like no other breed (in my opinion). 

We can learn a lot from dogs. And other animals and our interactions w/them -not just observing them. 

Future episode with expert dog neuroscientist who also is an expert on human learning coming soon to the Huberman lab podcast.

caption:
☕ Your morning coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up.

A new study published in JAMA followed more than 131,000 people for up to 43 years and found that drinking 2–3 cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with an 18% lower risk of dementia compared with drinking little or none.

People with higher caffeinated coffee intake were also less likely to report subjective cognitive decline and performed modestly better on certain measures of cognitive function.

The strongest associations were seen with moderate coffee intake—about 2–3 cups per day.

Researchers believe coffee's benefits may come from more than just caffeine. Coffee is rich in bioactive compounds, including polyphenols, that may help reduce inflammation and oxidative stress—two processes that are closely linked to brain aging. 

This doesn't mean coffee prevents dementia or guarantees protection. This was an observational study, so it can't prove cause and effect. But it adds to growing evidence that the habits we practice consistently over decades can influence brain health as we age.

Your daily habits matter. Sleep. Exercise. Blood sugar control. A nutrient-dense diet. Strong social connections. And yes... your morning cup of coffee may be one small piece of the puzzle. ☕🧠

caption:
GET YOUR CORTISOL RHYTHM CORRECT: THE KEY TO ENERGY, SLEEP & HORMONE HEALTH •
-
It’s impossible to overstate the importance of getting your cortisol rhythm correct. Many people get this wrong, especially nowadays in the age of cortisol elevating artificial LED lights, late shifted schedules and the rest. 
-
In fact, most people qualify as shift workers which is known to have severe mental and physical health impacts. Obviously, we need shift workers and be grateful to them(!), but most people don’t have to do shift work, but are imposing that schedule on themselves. 
-
The key is to spike your morning cortisol within the first hour or two after waking. I explain how to do that in this post. 
-
It’s also important to have your cortisol low as you head toward bedtime and if you need to exercise or do intense activities or you have some stress later in the day you need to do things to bring that stress level down. 
-
Even if you can fall asleep, people who tend to wake up agter 3-4 hours of sleep feeling wide awake are generally struggling with their cortisol rhythm.
-
There are many zero cost practices to spike your morning cortisol & reduce your evening cortisol. I discussed those on the Huberman La podcast episode about cortisol. 
-
This post focuses mostly on the morning aspect. But things like NSDR, sauna, hot baths, hot shower prior to bedtime can help in the pm.
-
There are also a lot of misconceptions about cortisol. For instance, that caffeine increases cortisol. That’s not true for regular caffeine users. Same goes for deliberate cold exposure. It does not increase cortisol if you do it a couple times a week or more. If anything has the opposite effect!
-
To find the podcast go to hubermanlab.com and put cortisol into the search function. It’s time stamped so you can navigate quickly to the topics most of interest to you. We’re now video on all formats. YouTube, Spotify, and X and audio only on Apple.

Plastic blenders are a source of microplastics that most people overlook.

Those with plastic jars or pitchers release microplastics, and even nanoplastics, into blended food or drinks due to friction and mechanical abrasion during blending.

A single 30-second blending cycle can release up to 1 billion (yes, with a “b”) micro- and nanoplastic particles.

BPA-free products are safer but can still release particles due to heavy use, heat, or abrasion. My advice is to switch to a completely stainless-steel blender. It’s the only way to avoid contamination.

Thanks to @steven for allowing me to audit his kitchen! Check out the full episode.

caption:
There are things I’ve stopped chasing, because I’ve seen what they actually do to the human body — and I can’t unsee it.

Here’s what I willingly go without:

Ultra-processed food. This is the one that matters most. 73% of the American food supply is ultra-processed. These products are engineered by food scientists to override your hunger signals, hijack your dopamine system, and keep you eating past the point of fullness. I don’t eat them because I’ve watched what they do to my patients — and what they were quietly doing to me. 

Skipping movement. Exercise is mitochondrial medicine. It’s the single most powerful intervention we have for insulin sensitivity, neurogenesis, mood regulation, and longevity. At 66, I am in the best shape of my life and that did not happen by accident.

Neglecting my brain. Cognitive decline is not inevitable. It is largely driven by lifestyle — blood sugar dysregulation, chronic inflammation, poor sleep, sedentary behavior, nutritional deficiencies. What you do in your 40s, 50s, and 60s determines what your brain looks like in your 80s. 

Alcohol. I’m not rigid about it. A glass of wine with good friends, good food, good conversation — sometimes that’s medicine too. But the one-off drink that fragments my sleep, tanks my HRV, and clouds my thinking the next morning is a trade that stopped making sense a long time ago.

Chronic stress. I’m not immune to it. At 66, I’m still writing, seeing patients, traveling, building. Stress is part of the job. The difference is I no longer let it sit in my body unchecked. Chronic, unmanaged stress raises cortisol, suppresses immune function, shrinks the hippocampus, disrupts sleep, and accelerates aging at the cellular level. 

After 30 years in functional medicine, I’ve made these trades because the return is undeniable — energy, clarity, strength, sleep, resilience, and a body that functions the way it was designed to.

You don’t have to give up everything. But you do have to get honest about what things are actually costing you.

MOST DOGS NEED FAR MORE EXERCISE THAN THEY CURRENTLY ARE GETTING TO BE HAPPY & HEALTHY •
-
Cesar Milan aka the Dog Whisperer was my guest on the recent Huberman Lab podcast. 

Most people do not walk their dogs enough and it causes their dogs to be anxious and unhealthy much of the time. 
Most dogs need at least 30 min brisk walks (and up to 60 min or more) twice per day every day. Some breeds need far more. 

Tiring out your dog is so crucial to their wellbeing. The daily walks are of course also good for you. People often ask me if the morning sunlight viewing I always talk about for humans pertains to animals too and the short answer is yes: absolutely — same neurons in the eyes and brain govern the improved mood and sleep that morning sun viewing triggers.

I raised both my bulldog-mastiffs (and pit) mutts using Cesar’s methods and they worked terrifically well both times… and that is a stubborn (and in the case of Strummer, my second dog also super energetic) breed.

The 2, 45-60 min structured walks per day were/are what  is needed and often a good 4mike hike on the weekend and mid week too. 

People debate dog training methods but to my knowledge, everyone agrees that dogs need exercise. Also, the vets I consulted (I have one in my family!) confirmed most people just don’t exercise their dogs nearly enough. 

The episode with Cesar covers: selecting the right dog, setting your energy to lead your dog, knowing how much to exercise your dog, fixing behavioral issues, and much more.

I’m going to explain the limitation of all scientific studies if you want to listen with an open mind.

The human body is complex. When we consume something, it can affect many biomarkers and biological pathways at once. But in a randomized controlled trial, researchers cannot measure every single biomarker that changes in the body because it is simply not statistically feasible.

So they can only choose a narrow set of metrics, basically a small percentage of what may actually be changing. For creatine, they may track things like strength, muscle mass, kidney markers, etc. Based on those selected metrics, creatine may look fine.

But that does not mean the entire biological picture was captured. Some long-term tradeoffs or side effects will go unnoticed because replicating the true treatment effect of all biomarkers isn't statistically possible. If it were, no "scientifically proven" supplement or drug would be pulled back from the market.

Absence of side effects in a limited-scope study does not rule out the possibility of side effects in the human body.

caption:
It’s okay to add a banana to your blueberry smoothie. Bananas are nutritious, I eat them, and this is not a reason to stop. But if your goal is to preserve as many of the berry polyphenols as possible, the chemistry matters. 
 
A small, acute study in eight healthy men compared standardized cocoa flavan-3-ols consumed alone, in a banana smoothie, or in a mixed-berry smoothie. The banana smoothie reduced circulating epicatechin metabolites by approximately 80%, whereas the berry smoothie produced levels similar to the flavan-3-ols consumed alone. 

The culprit was polyphenol oxidase, or PPO, an enzyme that oxidizes certain polyphenols when plant tissue is blended. 

- Banana: approximately 3,258 units of PPO activity per 100 grams
- Avocado: approximately 24 units per 100 grams
- Blueberry: approximately 12 units per 100 grams

This does not mean a banana eliminates every beneficial compound in blueberries. Blueberries contain many other polyphenols, including anthocyanins, and this was a small study that should be replicated. But the magnitude of the effect was meaningful enough for me to consider when optimizing my smoothie. 

My solution is simple: I replace the banana with avocado. 
 
Per 100 grams, avocado contains approximately 95% less sugar, more than twice the fiber, about 36% more potassium, and more folate, vitamin K, and niacin than banana. It also contains substantially more monounsaturated fat (and therefore more calories) which may not align with everyone’s goals. 
 
For me, that fat is another advantage. I add kale to my smoothie, which is rich in lutein. Lutein accumulates in the retina and the brain, where it contributes to visual and cognitive function. Human studies have found that adding avocado to a carotenoid-rich meal can substantially increase lutein (more than 5-fold) and beta-carotene absorption. 

So this is not about labeling bananas as “bad.” It is about matching the ingredient to the objective, which is polyphenol optimization (for me).

caption:
This is a big deal. Omega-3s reduce aggressive behavior across randomized controlled trials.

A meta-analysis of 29 studies and nearly 4,000 participants found that omega-3 supplementation reduced aggressive behavior by up to 28%. The benefit was broadly consistent across children and adults, males and females, community and clinical samples, and across high and low omega-3 doses and treatment durations. It also helped with both reactive/impulsive and proactive/planned aggression.

Mechanistically, this makes sense. Omega-3s are deeply involved in brain cell membranes, neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, cerebral blood flow, and gene regulation. DHA is especially enriched in the prefrontal cortex, which is critical for impulse control, emotion regulation, and executive function.

The authors even concluded that there is now “sufficient evidence” to begin implementing omega-3 supplementation to reduce aggression in the community, the clinic, or the criminal justice system. That’s a remarkable statement for a nutritional intervention and a reminder that omega-3s influence brain health and may also shape behavior in meaningful ways.

Study title:
“Omega-3 supplementation reduces aggressive behavior: A meta-analytic review of randomized controlled trials”

caption:
RUCKING & NATURE •
-
I started going to Yosemite almost as soon as I got my drivers license and I got hooked on backpacking and hiking there from go. It’s one of my favorite homes on earth. 
-
My favorite hike in all of the park is Clouds Rest which is up in the high country Meadows. It is about 15 miles round-trip from Sunrise trail head it takes you up to just shy of 10K feet with 360 degree views way above Half Dome. 
-
I used to head up Clouds Rest near my birthday and do my age in push-ups but this year I decided to ruck it (thank you @michael_easter for the inspiration!) and it was brutal, but awesome. (Truth told I was over ambitious, packed ~85lbs and drank about 10 to 15 pounds of that as water and @mateina before heading down, so the descent was easier. It wasn’t quite a Masogi (50% chance of failure) but it was painful enough (see last video in carousel; I’m fried). 
-
Mike Easter was on the podcast a little while ago talking about carrying weight over distance and how transformative it is for the mind and body and I couldn’t agree more. It goes way beyond a “workout” when you’re not sure you can complete it. 
-
If you haven’t been to Yosemite this year or ever it’s incredible as always, the crowds are really low, and the vegetation and animals are out in full burst. Go!
-
If you decide to do Clouds Rest, do your research prior. You’ll need to bring a lot of water(!). There are very few/0 water sources along the hike and unlike Glacier Natl Park etc, at Yosemite high country there isn’t much info on what to do/watch for, just bear-food stash warnings galore, so a lot of people just hike out and don’t go prepared and have to U Turn. Water and head lamps are necessary. 
-
And the final ascent is rather precarious. You don’t need to be a mountaineer, but if you’re afraid of heights or if there’s any rain or gusty wind, you’ll want to take extra extra precaution and maybe wait for better conditions. Don’t mess with nature. She almost always wins. 
-

No HIPAA means your blood work, your health history, your biometrics don't get the legal protection you'd assume comes standard with anything medical. Their own policy says they can disclose your info to law enforcement or government agencies whenever they decide it's "necessary," no warrant needed. They can also sell your de-identified health data for basically any business purpose, and if the company ever gets acquired or merges, your data transfers right along with the sale like any other asset. To be fair, they do say your health data isn't used to train their AI models, which is more than some companies commit to. But that one good clause doesn't cancel out the rest. caption:
DO TELL. NO EXPLANATION NEEDED (BUT FEEL FREE TO ELABORATE IF YOU WANT) •
-
A new year is not just another day and trip around the sun. A unique feature of the human brain is that we don’t just hold memories of past and perceive things in the present, we can anticipate things far into the future and carry out plans according to how we think we’ll feel in the future. 
-
New Year’s resolutions are good example of us segmenting time and making plans. 
-
I think that’s great. I add one “do more of X” and one “eliminate Y”, each year. (Sometimes several of each, and I write them down, and I check back at the end of the year to see if I held up to it.) 
-
I was struck by a post from @danielpink who’s an expert in the data on behavioral change. He mentioned that one word thematic titles about a new year and what we want from ourselves in that year can have a bigger impact than an unframed list of changes, but it’s good to have a list of specific changes as well. 
-
Apparently a one word thematics can help frame it all and keep you on track. That makes sense; we all get busy… within a few weeks everyone will be talking about Valentine’s Day or whatever and the notion that we’re in a new year seems to vanish. Returning to a one word theme is doable.
-
So… I’m on board this one word thematic idea even if it’s just to remind us of the specific changes to make. 
-
I know what mine is. I’m genuinely curious: what’s your one word theme for 2026? For you not for all of humanity!
-
If you want to share the specific changes you plan to make as resolutions that’s great too. I like to think people learn from each other’s plans. I certainly do.
-
And… more solo and guest episodes of the Huberman Lab podcast are on the way with all new topics for 2026. I’ll also be showing up some in new media venues as well. The HLP will continue with Monday full length episodes, and Thursday “Essentials” episodes, which are 30 minute essential only takeaways.
-
Please put any questions or guests or topic suggestions in the comments below. I do review those. And thank you for your interest in science!

caption:
If you could invest in one thing to live a longer, healthier, and happier life, what would it be?

For more than 85 years, researchers at Harvard followed hundreds of people across their entire lives, tracking everything from their physical health and mental well-being to their careers, relationships, and aging. It became the longest-running study of adult development in history.

After decades of data, one finding stood above the rest:

The strongest predictor of a long, healthy, and fulfilling life wasn't wealth, fame, social status, cholesterol levels, or genetics.

It was the quality of your relationships.

The people who were most connected to family, friends, and community lived longer, stayed healthier, and were happier as they aged. In fact, participants who were most satisfied in their relationships at age 50 were the healthiest at age 80.

The researchers also found that close relationships helped protect the brain. People with strong, supportive connections experienced less cognitive decline and maintained better memory and mental function later in life.

Investing in meaningful relationships may be one of the most powerful things you can do for your longevity, happiness, and overall well-being.

caption:
THE ABILITY TO SLEEP DESPITE STRESS: NSDR IS A POWER TOOL TO RESET (THAT ALSO TEACHES YOU HOW TO BE A BETTER SLEEPER) 

Sleep is the foundation of mental health, physical health, and performance. Most people need between six and nine hours of sleep to function well. 

One of the key markers of resilience (in the long run) is the ability to sleep despite typical or greater than typical stressors during the day.

To fall asleep, we need to turn off our thoughts and prevent our mind from racing: about plans, about the past, about the position of our body, about sounds in the room etc. 

Yet “turning off one’s thoughts” isn’t really possible. In fact, recent data show that people can actually track time and solve simple math problems in their sleep. So your mind is always active. 

The key to falling asleep is to stop thinking about doing and planning and to get into sensation. The problem with being in pure sensation is that we notice any minor discomfort related to limb position or temperature, etc. So what to do?(!)

Non-sleep deep rest or NSDR is the term that I came up with a few years ago to explain some of the core elements of a practice called Yoga Nidra. (NSDR doesn’t include mystical language for instance). NSDR is an amazing tool. 

Firstly, NSDR is not meditation. Meditation is a focusing exercise; it actually won’t help you sleep. 

NSDR is not a nap! Naps don’t teach us how to sleep at night, and in fact can disrupt our nighttime sleep, and circadian rhythms (although a short nap of 30 minutes or less is fine). 

NSDR resets mental and physical vigor and it teaches you how to be a better sleeper too. 

It takes just 10-30min. We have zero cost, zero signup NSDRs at: hubermanlab.com/nsdr 

(My voice but there are also links to NSDRs by @kelly.boys if you prefer a woman’s voice). 

I discovered NSDR in 2017 and only wish I had sooner. I do it every day. You can do it ANY time of day or night. 

And as always, thank you for your interest in science! 

@hubermanlab @stanford.med @stanford 

#neuroscience #science #ciencia #neurociência #resilience #sleep #nsdr

- Why endometriosis and adenomyosis affect millions of women yet take an average of 6 years to diagnose: the barriers driving that delay, how non-invasive imaging is replacing surgical diagnosis, and why a routine ultrasound is not sufficient to rule either condition out

caption:
Do not eat these. Discard immediately if you recognize any of these in yours or a loved one’s kitchen, it’s the easiest act of love you can do for them today.

A French study in PLOS Medicine examined the impact of emulsifiers (food additives used to improve texture and extend shelf life) on cancer risk.

Researchers analyzed data from 92,000 adults over nearly 7 years and found that certain emulsifiers significantly increased cancer risk:

Mono & diglycerides of fatty acids (E471)—found in processed baked goods, margarine, and ice cream—were linked to:
15% higher risk of overall cancer
24% higher risk of breast cancer
46% higher risk of prostate cancer

Carrageenan (E407 & E407a)—a thickening agent in dairy alternatives, deli meats, and plant-based products—was linked to:
32% higher risk of breast cancer.

Cancer is complex and multifactorial, but one thing is certain: the food we eat plays a massive role in shaping our long-term health. Cutting out ultra-processed foods and focusing on whole, nutrient-dense foods is one of the most powerful steps you can take to reduce disease risk.

Thank you to my friend Vani Hari for this image + bringing awareness to this critical issue.

caption: Hey everyone, I’m preparing for a podcast next week with my friend Jeff Cavaliere (@athleanx). Please share questions or topics you’d like us to explore in the comments.

INSPIRATION, DAILY EFFORT & (NO) EXCUSES •
-

I saw this when @gasmoney1 posted it (he has some great content on life design and aligning your work with deep meaning etc) and in addition to the impressive nature of the physical output of his 90 year old grandfather, a couple other things are extra cool/inspiring about it. 

1) he’s with family. It’s not in either-or. @athleanx @jockowillink @ken_rideout @cameronrhanes @drgabriellelyon = just few examples of those that have that balance And now @jellyroll615 too! 2) @gasmoney1 told me that his grandfather just “does something physical every day”; and he still works. I dont know if he spent time in the gym (maybe, I didn’t ask but ), but he certainly puts in physical effort and has for his entire life. Daily investment pays off. 

3) He is laughing and having fun while pushing. This is so vital. When I was in my teens, the best advice I got about exercise was “learn to enjoy training really hard”. 

I internalized that and I also applied it to school and work and yes, you still need to learn how to relax and recreate! but you really can learn to enjoy working hard. As my colleague @draliacrum at Stanford says “a mindset is a setting for your brain” (so simple but so apt!)… a hard work is fun mindset will make your life so much better.

caption:
A POWERFUL BUT RARELY DISCUSSED TOOL:
AMPLIFY YOUR MORNING CORTISOL LEVELS TO
LOWER THEM AT NIGHT •
-
Few things are more powerful than making sure that your morning cortisol levels are high and your evening and nighttime cortisol levels are low. This creates a synergistic effect on everything people are seeking: improved daytime mood, focus, and alertness, better ability to learn… and better sleep.
-
Proven ways to increase your morning cortisol include:
1) caffeine and hydration 
2) viewing bright light, ideally from morning sunlight
3) moderate to high intensity exercise
4) social interaction and even a bit of stress
-
You’ll want to avoid these things in the evening and at night. If you exercise at night, avoid excessive caffeine intake prior to it. If you train at night do something afterwards to lower your heart rate and bring your cortisol level down (long exhale breathing, physiological sighs, NSDR etc). 
-
Deliberately amplifying your morning cortisol peak, and deliberately lowering it in the late afternoon and evening has immediate and long-term effects, and these things synergize with one another.
-
I’ll cover it more in a future episode of the podcast, but it’s been shown that moderate to high intensity exercise at night actually lowers the next morning cortisol peak, and this can start to cascade where people just don’t feel well much of the day (anxiety etc). I still think it’s best to exercise rather than not exercise, but understanding this general contour of cortisol across the 24 hour cycle can be very beneficial.
-
A key point is that if your morning cortisol peak is not high enough, it tends to flatten out into the afternoon and make you more prone to stress.
-
Again: high morning cortisol and low night time cortisol = good! Get it!
-
If you have any questions or comments about this topic or guests or topics that you’d like me to cover on future Huberman Lab podcasts, please put those in the comment section below this post.
-
And as always, thank you for your interest in science!

caption:
I was diagnosed with autoimmune hypothyroidism at age 21. I’m 48 now, so this has been part of my body for 27 years.

What most people don’t realize is the thyroid and the stomach are closely linked in autoimmunity. When one is affected, the other often follows. There’s even a clinical name for it (thyrogastric syndrome) first described in the 1960s.

A recent bidirectional endoscopy revealed autoimmune gastritis. It’s the same underlying autoimmune tendency I’ve lived with since 21, now showing up in my stomach.

I’ve been so touched by all the thoughtful messages I’ve received over the past few days. 

I’m excited to tackle this diagnosis and share all my findings with you 🫶

A note to myself:
The Sun is rising for me
The Moon is shining for me
The wind is blowing for me
The rain is raining for me
The snow is snowing for me
The sea is breathing for me
The sand is getting warm for me
The flowers are blooming for me
The birds are singing for me
The music is created for me to dance to it

Everything here exists to entertain my senses. This world is created for me to FEEL it.

And yet, all of that serves as a trap. This planet is a venus flytrap for souls. We're seduced by its beauty, but more than that we're seduced by the opportunity to experience the most incredible thing - physical love. That is the actual bait souls are caught by. To kiss your child, to hug your lover, to be held by your parent, to laugh with your best friend- all of that is so tempting you can't resist it. So you incarnate in this realm, and bam💥- welcome to the world of suffering disguised as love and beauty to enjoy all of the above before it is taken from you. So cruel!

Feel free to borrow that note and keep it as a reminder. 
Don't waist your time, enjoy all of that while you can, even though there's underlying bitterness of a loss present in every second of your life here.
It's eased when you are able to generate that love from inside yourself and shower Your Self with it. Nothing is as liberating and invigorating as self-love.

caption:
Can you reverse gray hair? A new study out of Columbia University says yes — and what it reveals about stress and aging is remarkable.

Researchers digitized individual hairs at such high resolution they could map roughly one hour of growth at a time, then cross-referenced them with participants' stress diaries. 

The reversal window is real but finite. The study found it can happen in as little as 3 to 7 days, with a median of around 3 months — but only before the hair crosses its biological tipping point. 

Once it's far enough past that threshold, reversal is no longer possible.

Please note that this is just ONE study: gray hair can absolutely be genetic, caused by age, etc. but how fascinating is the research?

What do you think of this? Let me know in the comments 👇

Source: Rosenberg et al. (2021). Quantitative mapping of human hair greying and reversal in relation to life stress. eLife. doi.org/10.7554/eLife.67437

caption:
Supplementing with protein during strength training can increase gains in muscle size by approximately 27%, even when baseline protein intake is already considered adequate.

The current RDA for protein, 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day, is meant to prevent deficiency, not to optimize muscle growth or performance. Increasing intake to 1.5x the RDA leads to greater improvements in both muscle size and strength when combined with resistance exercise.

Doubling the RDA is even better. Meta-analyses suggest that around 1.6 g/kg/day of protein is sufficient to maximize gains in muscle strength and fat-free mass, with potential (though smaller) benefits observed at higher intakes up to 2.2 g/kg/day for those aiming to fully optimize muscle growth and recovery (like athletes).

This highlights how conservative the RDA truly is and why higher protein intakes are important, particularly for individuals engaging in regular strength training or other forms of physical activity.

caption:
Having your last meal at least 3 hours before bed improves blood pressure, heart health, and even blood glucose regulation.

Participants who stopped eating 3+ hours before sleep (extending their overnight fast to 13-16 hours) improved overnight diastolic blood pressure dipping by 3.5% and overnight heart rate by 5%. They also had a higher (better) HRV, lower cortisol, and improved insulin sensitivity.

That was without changing what or how much they ate!

This is one strategy I’ve advocated for years, so it’s promising to see further support from a controlled study on “sleep-aligned” eating patterns.

What you eat matters. But so does when.

caption:
В моем профиле вы могли видеть, что я практикую Рейки. Хочу вам сообщить, что я убираю модальность Рейки из описания своей деятельности.
Сейчас объясню почему. Мои руки и моя энергетика имеют свойство исцелять, убирать боль, снимать напряжение в теле, приносить ясность в сознание и убирать энергетические блоки. Так было всегда, сколько я себя помню. С раннего детства мои руки были горячие, мне было жарко в варежках в самую холодную зиму и я их скидывала.
У моего папы были такие руки, видимо передалось от него. Мы с ним по очереди помогали маме при ее сильнейших мигренях, когда лекарства ее не спасали. Мы просто массировали ей голову, думали боль проходит от массажа. Но это было свойство нашей энергии на самом деле.
Я никогда не знала про Рейки. Когда переехала в Лондон, случайно увидела книгу одного мастера Рейки и узнала про такой вид энергопрактики. Оказалось, он живёт в 5 остановках метро от меня. Конечно же я поехала к нему. Оказалось, что тут есть целая академия неизвестного мне до того момента какого-то Рейки, которую он создал. Я записалась на обучение. Там учили тому, что я умела делать интуитивно. Единственное, что было для меня новое - это работа на дистанции. Вот это было круто! В последствии, у меня были клиенты аж в Австралии. Работа на дистанции так же эффективна как и напрямую. Все это происходило еще в 2017 году.
Так вот, что я хочу вам сказать: за последние десять дней произошёл мощный апгрейд моих способностей. 
Сам по себе. Ночи напролёт я не могла спать, мои руки горели и как будто готовы были взорваться изнутри. Затем это прошло. 
На днях ко мне подсела младшая дочь и пожаловалась на усталость и головную боль. Она просто прилегла рядом и я положила ей руку на лоб. Через пять минут она уже спала. А через 20 проснулась свежая и без боли.
Продолжение⬇️

caption:
SET YOUR FOUNDATION OF PHYSICAL & MENTAL HEALTH BY SETTING YOUR CORTISOL RHYTHM •
-
Everyone would like to wake up feeling energized, in a good mood and able to focus on their activities for the day, including push back on stress as needed, and then relax into a terrific nights sleep. These are the hallmarks of excellent physical and mental health. Cortisol is really at the foundation of all of it.
-
Everyone has a natural 24 hour circadian rhythm in cortisol whereby their levels of cortisol vary dramatically across the 24 hour cycle. This is independent of stress. 
-
There’s an abundance of data showing that when your cortisol levels are elevated significantly in the morning and lower in the afternoon and at night, it supports robust daytime energy and focus, improved mood, ability to combat infections, and excellent sleep. 
-
There are numerous ways to increase morning cortisol, especially in the 2hrs after waking. Some are listed on the slide and the details are on the Huberman lab podcast out now.
-
It’s advantageous to keep your cortisol low in the evening and at night. Even if you exercise at night, that is possible. I explain the protocols for lowering cortisol at night in the episode as well.
-
It’s important to know that many people do the right things but at the wrong times with respect to cortisol. 
-
It’s also critical to point out that women’s and men’s cortisol rhythms (even pregnant women), are remarkably similar in overall 24hr pattern. This has been looked at many times. However, during the luteal phase of their cycle & menopause, there is a tendency for women’s cortisol rhythms to flatten: lower in the morning and higher in the pm. This can be offset using the tools listed on these slides. There are others as well. Discussed in the episode.
-
*NOTE: licorice root potently increases cortisol. Avoid at night and approach with caution! Licorice can raise blood pressure and is contraindicated with some meds. 
-

How Much Exercise Is Really Enough for Longevity?

This clip is from the video “How much time should a person spend exercising?“ which was released on my YouTube channel on 5/4/24.

“How much time do I need to spend exercising?” It’s a question I hear often, and it is the subject of countless research studies and popular press articles. And yet, this question misses the point.

When it comes to exercise, we should only concern ourselves with duration insofar as it influences what we really care about: results. Exercise is not a goal in itself – rather, it is a means of achieving good cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, and metabolic health, and the ultimate indicators of sufficient exercise are therefore a good VO2 max and adequate muscle mass.

caption:
WHY YOU WAKE UP JUST BEFORE YOUR ALARM CLOCK GOES OFF •
-
Cortisol is an amazing hormone. Yes, it helps you combat stress by mobilizing energy to your brain and body, but it also is a key player in coordinating when you’re alert, and when you tend to be more relaxed, etc. 
-
Cortisol is somewhat unique because it undergoes what is called an endogenous circadian rhythm. Meaning, it undergoes fluctuations from very high to very low across the 24 hour cycle. But… Cortisol is also released in response to things like stress, alarm clocks, even somewhat to a meal. Those increases in cortisol tend to be transient and ride atop the endogenous 24 hour rhythm.
-
Your SCN- a small cluster of neurons above the roof of your mouth coordinates the endogenous rhythm but remarkably, it can also learn to anticipate or what is called “entrain” to regularly occurring cortisol stimulating events- like alarm clocks that always go off at the same time.
-
So the simple answer to the question of why you awake up just before your alarm clock is “cortisol” but that really doesn’t get to the mechanism, which is why it took me about 2 1/2 minutes to explain. 
-
Biology is amazing. Just think about what’s required to coordinate these events among distant parts in the body and brain and trillions of cells… incredible. 
-
Also, thanks to @chadwright278 for asking me to look into this mechanism. I’m only about a year late in answering! Better late than never, right Chad?
-
Meanwhile, if you have any questions or comments about this or other topics (or guests you’d like to see me to host on the Huberman lab podcast), please put them in the comments section below.
-
And as always, thank you for your interest in science!

caption:
You could be 40 or 50 years away from knowing whether your habits paid off. Or you could look at your walking pace right now.

A new study followed nearly 4,000 adults in their 80s and found that the fastest walkers, people moving quicker than 93 percent of their peers, were 50 percent less likely to develop cognitive impairment, and 60 percent less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s or another dementia. Brain scans backed it up: these fast walkers had slower memory decline and better-preserved hippocampal volume, the brain region most tied to memory.

Walking briskly requires your brain, heart, lungs, and nervous system to coordinate in real time. Losing that coordination may be one of the earliest signs your brain is changing.

Luckily gait speed is trainable. Focus on cadence, not just stride. Add short bursts of brisk walking a few times a week. Strengthen your hips and core. Swing your arms.

Swipe through to see the full study, and what to start doing today.

caption:
Most people think liver issues come from alcohol.

But one of the most common liver conditions in the US has nothing to do with your favorite cocktail.

It’s called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MΑSLD)—and nearly 1 in 3 adults has it.

One of the biggest drivers: drinking diet sodas and sugary drinks.

The problem? Early MASLD rarely shows symptoms, so it can be easy to miss.
That’s why deeper testing of liver function, metabolic health, and systemic inflammation matters.

Test & track:
- Liver stress: ALT, AST, GGT, ALP
- Metabolic health: Glucose, Insulin, HbA1c
- Inflammation levels: hs-CRP

MASLD isn’t an alcohol problem.
It develops from patterns over time. 

The good news? Early detection and healthy habits can go a long way toward preventing or possibly even reversing MASLD.

Not medical advice. Consult a medical professional with any medical questions. For marketing purposes only.

Comment SAUNA & I’ll DM you a 30min ESSENTIALS (key takeaways only) episode on deliberate heat exposure for health. 

The sauna has known benefits for cardiovascular health, growth hormone release, and more. I’ve covered that on several episodes of the Huberman Lab podcast, including the essentials episode out now, which hits all the key points in 30 minutes.

One important reason to cover your head in the sauna is otherwise jt will make your hair brittle. Heat denatures proteins. Many people who enjoy the sauna notice that their hair gets brittle. No it’s not reversible but yes, your hair grows out. 

This is not a problem with infrared sauna because IR saunas tend not to get hot enough to have this effect. I’m referring to traditional wet or dry sauna. There’s a reason why at Russian Banyas the men and the women cover their heads with wool caps!

The other reason is to insulate your brain, which allows you to stay in longer more comfortably and still get the benefits. Obviously you don’t want to crank up the temperature so high that you burn yourself but approach this rationally and you should be fine. All the usual precautions apply still: that pregnant women shouldn’t be exposed to high heat, men wishing to conceive in the next 90 days should be aware of the DNA mutation effects of heat, etc. 

You can simply put a towel over your head or use wool cap. 

My favorite sauna protocol is three rounds of 20 minutes, each at high heat (for me 210F+; but I’m very heat adapted; you may not be so be safe!), 3min cold plunge in between each round. And yes I’m ruddy (vasodilated) here in this video b/c of that!

caption:
Higher meat intake was associated with less cognitive decline and lower dementia risk in APOE e4 carriers, a group at higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease and dementia.

Those who ate ~2 servings of meat per day had a better 10-year cognitive trajectory and a 55% lower dementia risk compared to people eating less than a half a serving per day.

That pattern wasn’t seen in the non-APOE e4 carriers and was NOT observed for processed meat. Unprocessed red meat alone was also linked to lower dementia risk in APOE e4 carriers.

My take is not “everyone should eat more meat.”

But a few servings per day of unprocessed meat (as observed in this study) is perfectly healthy for most people.

Should you stop eating produce? No. We should be much more upset about how widespread these chemicals have become, especially when children are being exposed through foods we otherwise consider healthy.

caption:
NEUROPLASTICITY: THE 4 STEPS TO LEARNING •
-
STEP 1: ALERTNESS 
Aside from developmental plasticity, which sets up basic sensory functions like our ability to see and hear, etc., all forms of neuroplasticity  and learning require us to be alert. That is, in a state of slightly (or greatly) elevated autonomic arousal. But if arousal is too high, the next step doesn’t happen and it must….

2) FOCUS 
It is an absolute truth that whatever we focus our perceptual attention on is what stands the best chance to be remembered. That could be a process, a fact, a contingency like when and how often rewards arrive or punishments arrive… all of that shapes behavior. (by the way if you’re wondering what the best reward schedule is, it’s intermittent… ~random reward intervals. 

3) AGITATION (FROM ERRORS!)
This is the hardest one for people to embrace. In the absence of errors, your nervous system has no reason to change. Please read that twice. 

But why? What do errors actually do? They change the neurochemical environment in the areas of your nervous system that need to change. You need to embrace the agitation that comes from errors. That doesn’t mean you need to be stressed, but you need to feel enough agitation that it allows you to dial your focus in deeper on the things you’re trying to learn.

4) SLEEP & TIME
The rewiring of your nervous system largely takes place during sleep. In particular, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. That form of sleep that predominates the last 1/3rd of your night. If you want to rewire your brain: for new skills, to alter your emotional relationship to an experience of past or in the present or future anticipated experience, you need the sleep that comes the night after learning attempts. 

Strummer sleeps in front of a @saunaspace red light (no affiliation but love their red incandescents),
We do treadmill training twice a day. He’s doing it for intermittent reinforcement. Eventually reward will come at the end. He learned selfies the first time.

Thank you for your interest in science!

HAPPY 4th July and 250th Birthday USA •
-
Forever grateful to be born in this incredible country.

When you grow up the child of a first generation immigrant— as I did, you hear all the time about how incredible it is here, what aspects of it do and don’t exist elsewhere and how lucky we are to live here. 

The USA has a history of being supportive of science and engineering. That’s what brought my father here. My mother was already an American citizen. I am so grateful for their experiment that was me (and my siblings). 

And while that is my story and perspective … let’s not forget we are all mutts… there are no true pure breeds. … In fact, nature punishes that with deleterious mutations. 

So, despite all the divisiveness that exists nowadays, I remain optimistic that we will move this experiment forward toward the outcomes that continue to provide the most freedom and liberty for the greatest number of people …as long as they honor the freedoms and liberties of other people. That can be a complicated equation sometimes. But we can do it. We’ve made it this far. 

And for those of you not from the United States, every time I travel, I see aspects of other countries that I think we would be wise to incorporate here. That’s the whole point. This USA thing is an experiment and a relatively young one. It is still happening. We are the experiment. 

A couple of final points:
I don’t use a teleprompter. I never have here or on the podcast. Except for ad reads, of course where the language has to be precise down to the word, but I don’t blink much… that’s how I remember when I want to say. So ditch the notion that this is a teleprompter post or political in any way. I truly love this country and I’m a patriot. And I’m proud to say it. 

Wishing you all a happy and safe Fourth of July. Let’s keep moving this experiment forward! 

Thank you all and thank you USA for your interest in science!

caption:
The current physical activity guidelines are too low.

I’ve been saying this for a while. And a new study confirms it.

Meeting the standard 150 minutes/week was associated with only a modest ~8–9% lower cardiovascular risk.

The biggest protection occurred at roughly 560–610 minutes/week, about 3–4× higher, where cardiovascular risk was 30% lower.

One other interesting finding was that people with a higher cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max) needed less activity than people with lower fitness to achieve the same reduction in risk!

We need to distinguish between the minimal activity volume required for basic protection, and the substantially higher volumes required for optimal resilience.

LED BULBS DAMAGE MITOCHONDRIA & USING FULL SPECTRUM LIGHT TO IMPROVE MITOCHONDRIA •
-
OK, we have to be clear that blue light does not necessarily need to appear blue. I know that’s confusing but what we’re talking about is short wavelength light: and people use the term blue light as a proxy for that. 
-
Incandescent bulbs tend to be full spectrum meaning they emit short, medium, and long wavelengths. That is good because the long wavelengths improve your mitochondria and offset what appears to be the damage of short wavelengths. 
-
Sunlight, of course, is full spectrum. So getting sunlight in your eyes and on your skin each day can help offset some of the mitochondrial damage being done by LED bulbs. 

It’s also good for you in a number of other ways, including hormone health, energy, skin health, eyesight and much more. Obviously you don’t want a sunburn so don’t over expose yourself to UV. The best way to avoid doing that is to just check the UV index in your area.
-
Red light and infrared light devices can be very helpful, but are not necessary. If you can use incandescent bulbs at home do it but as a general rule: try and make your days as bright with sunlight as you can without getting a sunburn get outside in the am if possible and then work near a window if you can. 

And then at night really be mindful of not getting too much LED bulb exposure. Dim it down. Consider short wavelength blocking glasses. It’s not all about screens & sleep. It’s about mitochondria. 
-
My guest on the Huberman lab podcast out now is Dr. Glen Jeffery. He is the world expert on these topics. In the episode, we discuss the positive effects of certain wavelengths of light & zero cost, low cost & device related protocols that you can use to meaningfully improve your mitochondria with light.

caption:
“FACE PULLS”: SET YOUR DEFAULT POSTURE UPRIGHT, MAKE YOUR SHOULDERS AND NECK STABLE •

This week’s Huberman Lab podcast features Jeff Cavalier of  @athleanx — he’s a licensed physical therapist, strength and conditioning coach known for helping people reach their fitness goals, overcoming pain and injury with specific movements and getting tremendous longevity from their fitness training. 

We sat down and talked about “the little things that allow you to do the big important things for your entire life” on the podcast. 

Yes it’s true: You need to do the basics. Men and women should do basic compound movements of pressing and pulling and for their legs …and do so with progressive resistance. Every week. 

But the issue people tend to run into is pain or injuries or challenges with imbalanced mechanics. Doing certain little things for just a few minutes per week can be the difference between lifelong pain-free training, great posture (at default— without having to think about it!) better breathing, better mobility, and on and on.

One of the key movements that every man and woman should do a few times a week at least are “face pulls” which is where you pull a rope from slightly above high-level on a cable machine (or you could use bands if you don’t have access to a cable machine) starting from a position where your hands are almost touching directly in front of you (arms straight) to what sort of looks like a “double biceps flexed pose”, but with your thumbs pointed back and  bit out & away from your ears. That’s the correct “external rotation” you want, which is essential… you can learn more about on the podcast. 

All the texting and sitting that we do nowadays has most people defaulting to internal rotation, chin down and C shaped… not good (for many reasons!).

A video of how to do face pulls correctly as well as train your arms correctly are available at the “Huberman lab clips” channel on You Tube. There is a short excerpt of it here as well.

Thank you, Jeff for being such a tremendous coach in public educator helping people get and stay super fit. We appreciate you!

caption:
A daily multivitamin slows biological aging.

I take a multivitamin everyday and have done so for years. A new study that was part of the large COSMO trials just showed that older adults who took a standard multivitamin daily for two years slowed their biological aging by 2.7 to 5.1 months compared to adults given a placebo. It may sound like a modest effect but remember this was just after two years. Think of taking a multivitamin for 50 years or maybe since you were a kid. There will be a compounding effect! These COSMO trials also found that older adults taking a multivitamin for 3.6 years slowed global brain aging by 2.1 years and episodic brain aging by 4.9 years. Adults in the placebo group continued to accelerate their brain aging. Just one a day has that effect on brain aging! It is was a called a “low-hanging fruit” because it is easy to pick it and eat it and get the benefits. 

Do you want you and your family to be in the placebo group or the multivitamin group. You know my answer. Let’s do the things we can to fill some of the important micronutrient gaps we are not meeting from diet alone.

caption:
PLEASE WELCOME… STRUMMER. 
(Named after the Great @joestrummer of course; the Clash, Mescaleros) 

Strummer is 10 weeks old today. 

This is my second Olde English Bulldog. For those of you that have listened to the podcast for a while you may recall early episodes that featured Costello — also an Olde English Bulldog (which is distinct from pure English bulldog; Olde English are mutted with Mastiff and Pit, which yields pups that breathe better and move better). Costello passed (after a long life) in 2021. 

Strummer’s morning routine:
Wake up
Sunlight
Walk 
Training (yes we started training him right away. He can already Sit. Stay. Wait. And he knows to make eye contact. He’s learning most things in two trials… he’s very smart). We only use rewards and semi-intermittent reinforcement to train. 

Then we do a little bit of nose training: then… Free play. 
Then he eats breakfast. 
Water.
And then he gets a nap in front of a red incandescent light @saunaspace (no affiliation, but theirs are amazing.)

We repeat that routine in the evening.

Obviously, he does not need @mateina — the Yerba zero sugar, cold brew organic mate I helped develop, but I DO! (And I drink the loose leaf Mateina Yerba too, brewed hot). 

A few bulldog facts:

The Olde English line from the early last century and 1800s used for bullbaiting (thankfully a banned sport now) is different than the line that was revitalized in the 1970s, but the idea is similar: healthier bulldog breed, better breathing. 

Why?
Well, English bulldogs are wonderful animals, but excessive inbreeding has caused a lot of problems for the breed over the last 30 years. People get them and they don’t realize how much work and cost they are and the many medical problems that go with that inbreeding, such as apnea etc. The @bulldogclubofamerica & @americankennelclub breeders are working hard to restore health to the pure English Bulldog breed.

And I purposefully kept his tail!

caption:
Sitting on the ground more is one of the simplest things you can do for long-term mobility.

It sounds almost too basic, but getting down to the floor and back up is a real marker of independence. If you lose that ability, a lot of everyday function starts to go with it.

Sit with your legs straight out. Sit cross-legged. Kneel. Shift around. These positions gently restore hip rotation, ankle mobility, and the ability to move your body in and out of different shapes.

This kind of low-level, daily movement practice helps maintain better joint mechanics, and according to @thereadystate, it might be one reason why “floor cultures” such as those in Asia often preserve mobility longer and have fewer problems related to stiffness and loss of function.

From the latest episode of the FoundMyFitness podcast. Available on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.

Recently I appeared on @realtimers hosted by @billmaher to discuss zero cost behavioral practices to improve mental health and physical health. I put morning sunlight viewing (especially on overcast days) right up there with proper nutrition (eating mostly non-processed or minimally processed foods) and exercise (cardiovascular exercise and resistance training each 2-4x per week depending on your needs and schedule), as the key pillars of building and maintaining your mental and physical health, every age. -
We also discussed zero cost science supported tools to reduce your stress and improve sleep, and emerging changes in scientific funding and public health discourse more generally.
-

caption:
You may be paying a premium for avocado oil and getting cheaper oils instead.

A new UC Davis study found that 48 of 54 processed foods labeled with avocado oil, or 89%, also contained other oils such as canola and safflower.

Every salad dressing tested failed purity checks, along with 93% of chips and 71% of mayonnaises.

Importantly, this does not necessarily mean the brands knowingly misled consumers. Many food manufacturers purchase oils through third-party brokers or multiple suppliers. Lead researcher Selina Wang believes the adulteration likely begins with suppliers who blend avocado oil with less expensive oils before selling it as pure.

But brands still have a responsibility to test and verify the ingredients they purchase.

So what can you do?

Prioritize whole, minimally processed foods. Read the complete ingredient list instead of relying on front-of-package claims. Look for companies that independently test their oils and verify their suppliers. You can even contact a brand and ask whether it tests its avocado oil for authenticity.

We need stronger purity standards, independent testing, and accountability at every level. If avocado oil is the only oil listed on the label, that is what should be inside.

Source: Lopez-Alvarez et al., Applied Food Research (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.afres.2026.102389

caption:
WHY SOME PEOPLE STAND OUT AGAINST OTHER TOP LEVEL PERFORMERS •

On a recent episode of Huberman Lab, I hosted @portal.ido — savant of all things movement. 

We were discussing the science and mechanics of movement and  why some people stand out against the backdrop of other high performers in their sport or creative art, or even science. 

They do one thing (or everything) differently than the rest… and it ends up looking like no other. It captivates us. 

I gave several examples, two of which are noted here. The first is skateboarder @antwuandixon who was already amazing when he was a young kid, still is now (and has a recent amazing comeback story; search The Antwuan Dixon story on YTube), and the other is Michael Jordan. 

In each case they just make the same things other people do look so much better, so fluid and yet powerful and with signature style. 

The overall discussion was about the science and practice of different types of movement. 

We all have the same circuits for generating bodily movement. But somehow certain people are able to cultivate a seemingly perfect balance between smoothness and explosiveness, and something unique that defies words…and they stand out.

In science, it’s not about movement, but there have been a few scientists I can think of whose discoveries were presented in ways that were so visually impressive that they are burned not only into the textbooks but into the mind of every student who sees those images. It is as if the unique impact of their discovery was translated into the visual space. I have my favorite example from neuroscience and I’ll do a post about it soon. 

The Ido episode is a unique one and definitely one of my favorites I’ve hosted. You can find it by going to hubermanlab.com or on any podcast platform.

Feel free to put questions below. 

Also feel free to mention artists, athletes etc who you think stand out from rest because of something truly unique in their mechanics etc. Would love to learn about them as I’m sure others here might too.

Thank you for your interest in science!

🇬🇧Put down whatever you're currently reading and pick up The Wizard of Oz.
But don't read it as a children's book. Read it as a book for adults.
Look at the characters and compare them to yourself. What qualities do you believe you're missing? And then look at your life. How is it reflecting you back to yourself? How do you show up in it?
As you follow the heroes on their journey, reflect on your own story.
For a long time, I believed I lacked courage. Yet life repeatedly placed me in situations where I showed extraordinary bravery and resilience. At the same time, I kept encountering people who mirrored fear and hesitation back to me.
Everything is a mirror—just not always a straightforward one.
Perhaps a courageous soul comes here to experience fear. Deep down, you know you can stand your ground and face whatever comes your way, yet somehow you find yourself doing the opposite. Why? For what purpose?
Maybe simply to discover what it's like to walk in those shoes.
And here's something else to consider:
What is holding you back? What feels like a set of chains around your ankles? What do you believe is preventing you from fully spreading your wings? What limitations are you carrying?
Know this: they are imagined.
Any limitation placed upon your spirit is an illusion you have, for some reason, come to believe.
Seriously—set aside everything else you're reading and look at this book through the eyes of a modern adult.
To me, it feels incredibly relevant right now, at a time when we're being called to face our inner demons. Because this is a pivotal moment.
A moment of returning to our True Nature.
The time is coming when there will be less need to act out old programs, patterns, and roles—to pretend to be someone you are not. What will be required is something much simpler, and perhaps much more challenging:
To be your authentic self.
And if you've never truly known who that self is, then welcome.
These times are inviting us to find out.
The space I create helps my clients look themselves in the eye and gaze into their own souls.
And do you know the best part?
When people dare to look within, they discover their strength. ✨

caption:
WANT TO LEARN FASTER? UNDERSTANDING HOW NEUROPLASTICITY WORKS IS THE KEY & IT INVOLVES 4 (actually 5) CRITICAL STEPS •
-
ALL learning involves neuroplasticity, and while a lot has been discussed about this topic, most of what you see misses the mark in one or several ways.
-
To learn, 1) you need to be alert, and 2) you need to be focused. But those are just prerequisites. They are necessary, but not sufficient for learning. The critical step that triggers the actual rewiring of brain circuits that causes “learning” is… 3) ERRORS.
-
Errors and often the emotional frustration that accompanies them is what signals to your nervous system that something needs to change. It’s critical that you internalize that fact! It makes logical sense if you think about it. Why would your nervous system change if it could perform everything that you’re trying to do?
-
4) Actual circuit remodeling underlying learning occurs during sleep, in particular during rapid eye movement sleep (REM).
-
And then there’s the additional critical feature that most people overlook and that’s 5) mental reflection on the learning process and in particular self testing for what you did correctly and what you did incorrectly.
-
In fact, the data on how best to study and learn all point to self testing as an incredibly valuable, but under used tool.
-
In this post, I discussed the practical steps to trigger and enhance learning. I also discussed how to accelerate learning and how to make it more durable over time. It’s 4 key steps. (And one additional one to boost learning).
-
Perhaps test yourself and see if you can remember what those 4-5 steps are… if you can’t don’t worry, go back and read it again. Yes this is an example of what I’m trying to explain. But once it’s locked in, you’ll never forget it.
-
